title: Hungry for right (Matthew 5:6)
hook: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for what is right

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meek: strength held gently, like a horse that takes the bridle.

Hungry. Not a little peckish at four o'clock. Really hungry: a long hike, a fast, a day when everything went wrong and nobody remembered to eat. Or thirsty on a hot day, when water is the only thought left. The whole body leans toward one thing. Few things in a life get wanted like that: a person, a home, a cure, a child who comes back. The fourth line of the sermon names one more, and you can't eat it.
screen: `REALLY HUNGRY.` → `THIRSTY ON A HOT DAY.` → `WANTED LIKE WATER.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled." Righteousness can sound like a stiff, churchy word, even a little smug. But the Greek word, dikaiosune, is bigger and warmer. It means being right with God, and it also means justice: things set right between people. Greek uses one word for both. So does Hebrew: tsedakah, which is also the word Jews use for giving to the poor. So Jesus's listeners could hear both: a heart right with God, and a world where the widow gets fed and the worker gets paid. The prophet Amos put it like this: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Christians have leaned one way or the other at different times, and some hold both together: personal holiness and public justice. Now notice the verbs. Not blessed are the righteous. Blessed are the hungry for it: people who don't have it yet, who ache for it the way you ache for water. Nobody has to be finished. The blessing is on the wanting. And the promise: they shall be filled. The Greek word for filled, chortazo, is the one Matthew uses again when the crowds in the wilderness eat the loaves and fish and are filled. Not a taste. A full meal.
screen: `DIKAIOSUNE: RIGHT, AND JUSTICE.` · `LIKE A MIGHTY STREAM.` · `BLESSED ARE THE HUNGRY FOR IT.` · `FILLED: A FULL MEAL.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that isn't right: something big, like hunger, a war, an injustice in the news, or something close, like a family rift, a friend treated unfairly, something you did. Don't argue with it; just feel the hunger for it to be made right, and notice where you feel it in your body. If you pray, you can offer that hunger to God.
Righteousness. Dikaiosune in Greek: being right with God and things set right between people, one word for both.
Your line: hunger for good. Right with God and right between people: one word, one hunger. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians pursue righteousness both in personal prayer and repentance and in works of justice and charity: food banks, advocacy for the poor, and giving, which Christians in different churches see as part of the same calling.

chat.meaning: Dikaiosune means a heart right with God and justice between people. The blessing is on the hunger, and they shall be filled.

dikaiosune.meaning: Greek for righteousness and justice, one word

tsedakah.meaning: Hebrew for righteousness; also giving to the poor

Amos.meaning: a prophet: let justice run down as waters

chortazo.meaning: Greek for filled, as the crowds were with loaves
